A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained content can be matched despite substantial appendix expansion and figure renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-data, vision-language, and MultiBench experiments in Figures 4–9, Table 1, and Appendix D.

after.justification: V2 reports these empirical investigations with revisions, plus original robustness experiments, random-initialization controls, and MM-IMDb classification and fine-tuning results.

M1.justification: The original synthetic construction and independent unimodal encoders remain. Section 6.2 adds a bounded algorithmic application: fine-tuning CLIP encoders with L = L_sup + w L_CLIP, with supervised predictions from language embeddings. This introduces an explicit-alignment training objective without redesigning the original framework.

E1.justification: V2 adds MM-IMDb movie-genre prediction, including 23 binary tasks and fine-tuning experiments on 10 classes under scarce labels. It also replaces corrupted Wikipedia image-text inputs with semantically modified captions paired with unchanged images, materially changing the evaluated input conditions. The earlier synthetic and five MultiBench datasets remain.

E2.justification: The new MM-IMDb comparison evaluates supervised-only fine-tuning against combined supervised and CLIP training in Figure 10. Appendix D.3 adds randomly initialized network controls. The original pretrained vision and language model families are retained.

E3.justification: Wikipedia experiments replace random character deletion and Gaussian pixel substitution with GPT-generated semantic caption changes at 10–100% uniqueness. New protocols vary alignment metrics, alignment batch sizes of 256/512/1024, and the first encoder's depth. MM-IMDb uses 1024 examples per train/validation/test split and an explicit-alignment loss-weight sweep. Correlation metrics also change predominantly from Pearson to Spearman.

E4.justification: Appendices D.1–D.3 add tests of alignment-metric and batch-size sensitivity, deeper first-modality encoders, and randomly initialized networks. These examine measurement robustness, architectural dependence, and the role of training beyond v1's analyses. Figure 10 additionally tests sensitivity to explicit-alignment strength across movie genres.

E5.justification: Most plotted association estimates change from Pearson r to Spearman rho. The original five synthetic-data seeds and three MultiBench seeds remain unchanged; an increase in repeated runs is not documented. Figures 24–26 introduce a reporting inconsistency: plot labels use rho while captions still specify Pearson.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises retained correlations, including AVMNIST vision/audio values from 0.944/0.974 to 0.887/0.723. The replacement vision-language experiment reports Figure 8 slopes of 0.112, 0.071, and 0.024 at uniqueness levels 10, 50, and 90. Numerous robustness and MM-IMDb findings are added. Changed inputs and correlation metrics prevent interpreting these revisions as matched-setting performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: The alignment equations, synthetic-data definitions, independence assumptions, and illustrative prediction tables are retained. The bijection assumption is rephrased without changing its substance. No new theorem, proof, or theoretical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory findings, and substantive conclusion retain the claims that heterogeneity and uniqueness constrain alignment and that alignment does not universally predict performance. The new experiments support the existing practitioner implications rather than redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.1 replaces the interpretation that high corruption undermines the performance-capacity relationship with an account of flattening alignment-performance slopes while larger language models still perform better. Section 6.2 and Appendix D.7 add task-specific interpretations connecting alignment-performance slopes to the usefulness of explicit alignment.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 supplies the GPT-4o caption-generation prompt. Appendix A.4 documents MM-IMDb linear-probe tuning, 100-epoch probe training, and 30-epoch CLIP fine-tuning with learning rates, cosine scheduling, and warmup. Appendix A.1 newly discloses an alignment batch size of 512. These substantially extend procedural documentation; the code URL is unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Arevalo et al. (2017) for MM-IMDb. The alignment literature and positioning relative to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis remain substantively unchanged. Consolidating duplicate MultiBench references does not remove a distinct prior work.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Local revisions update the experimental setup and Section 5.1, subdivide Section 6, and reorganize the appendices around additional analyses. A forward-looking conclusion paragraph moves into the Impact Statement, and affiliation and proceedings information are updated.

P2.justification: Figure 6 replaces heatmaps with scatterplots against encoder depth minus transformation depth. V2 adds the MM-IMDb displays and extensive metric, batch-size, depth, and initialization panels. Previously separate vision-language figures are consolidated into Figures 27–28, and Figure 2 gains explanatory labels. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's empirical support through measurement-sensitivity and initialization controls in Appendices D.1–D.3 and a direct test of explicit-alignment weighting in Section 6.2. The documented semantic-caption manipulation also makes the intended intervention more interpretable than character/pixel corruption. These additions substantially strengthen robustness assessment and practical relevance. The Pearson/rho caption inconsistency in Appendix D.4 is a limited reporting drawback.
